title: Tech Stocks Slide Worldwide as Earnings Misses Revive Fears Over AI Spending
excerpt: The Nasdaq fell 1.83% on Thursday and Asian chip stocks tumbled on Friday as Alphabet, Amazon and Intel misses turned a company earnings story into a global repricing of AI spending.
body:
• Technology stocks fell across the United States, Europe and Asia on Thursday and Friday as a run of earnings misses revived fears that artificial intelligence spending is outrunning returns.
  • The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.83% on Thursday and South Korea's Kospi opened 3.11% lower on Friday, with SK Hynix down 6.36% and Samsung Electronics down 3.45%.
  • Alphabet fell 13.3% on Thursday after reporting negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion while keeping a $195 billion to $205 billion capital spending forecast; Amazon fell 6% in extended trading and Intel plunged 21% on a weaker outlook.
  • Microsoft was the counterpoint, rising after beating estimates on 48% Azure growth — a split that shows investors are now pricing AI returns company by company, not sector-wide.

Technology stocks slid across the globe on Thursday and Friday after earnings from major tech names in the United States and Asia reignited worries about how companies can make money from artificial intelligence. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.83% on Thursday, while the S&P 500 declined 0.62% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 184 points, according to Invezz. The selling then spread to Asia, where Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.68%, South Korea's Kospi declined 3.11% at the open and the Kosdaq dropped 2.35%, according to Mettis Global.

A selloff bigger than any one earnings report

This is no longer a story about a single company's quarter. In Japan, Advantest fell 5.43%, SoftBank Group declined 4.66% and Tokyo Electron dropped 3.93%. South Korea's semiconductor heavyweights suffered significant losses, with SK Hynix falling 6.36% and Samsung Electronics slipping 3.45%. On Wall Street, the broader semiconductor sector traded lower, with Nvidia down about 1.17% and AMD down 1.27% in Thursday trading, while semiconductor exchange-traded funds fell more than 2%. Fortinet shares fell 23% after its results, ServiceNow dropped 23.9% after missing profit estimates, and Marvell Technology declined 12.4%.

Funds exposed to the AI buildout have been hit for weeks. CoreWeave shares have fallen 30% in October amid rising bond yields and concerns about debt used to finance AI infrastructure, while Nebius is heading towards a 27% monthly decline. The Roundhill Memory ETF has declined 14% this month, and the iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF has lost 10%. As October's final trading session gets underway, the Nasdaq Composite is on track to lose 2.5% for the month.

The cash-flow question at the centre

Alphabet was the catalyst. Its shares fell 13.3% on Thursday after the Google parent missed expectations for earnings per share and revenue, a decline that threatened to erase more than $450 billion from its market value. The company reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion and maintained its full-year capital expenditure forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion, keeping investor attention fixed on the costs of its AI expansion.

Amazon added to the pressure in extended trading, falling 6% after reporting earnings and revenue below Wall Street estimates, negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion and a maintained 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $220 billion. Intel plunged 21% after issuing a weaker outlook for the current quarter, citing a slowdown in the personal computer market, with revenue from its client computing and physical AI group down 5% year on year to $8.1 billion.

Microsoft shows the other side of the trade

Microsoft provided a partial counterpoint. Its shares rose after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and earnings, supported by strong growth in its Azure cloud business, where revenue grew 48%. The split reaction — punishing heavy spenders whose cash flow has turned negative, rewarding the company whose cloud growth is covering its buildout — is the clearest sign yet that investors have stopped buying the AI story in bulk.

What this means for investors

For diaspora investors holding US tech through index funds, the immediate hit is index-level, not stock-specific: the Nasdaq's monthly decline is being driven by its largest constituents, so diversified holders feel it without owning any single name. The test ahead is cash flow. Companies that keep nine-figure capital spending forecasts while free cash flow stays negative will face the same repricing at the next earnings round, regardless of revenue growth.

What happens next

The market weakness also followed the Federal Reserve's decision on Wednesday to maintain its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%, with policymakers citing elevated inflation. Traders widely expect a rate rise at the Fed's December meeting, according to LSEG data cited by Invezz — a backdrop that raises the cost of the debt increasingly used to finance data centres, and keeps AI spending under scrutiny into the next earnings season.
